newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesian markets roiled by rupiah float.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesian markets roiled by rupiah float.

text.p: Indonesia succumbed to speculative attacks and floated the rupiah on Thursday, triggering steep declines in the currency and stock prices.

Bank Indonesia, the central bank, announced it was immediately ending its system of managing exchange rates through the use of an intervention band -- the parameters under which the bank stepped into the foreign exchange market.
The move made Indonesia the latest southeast Asian nation to cave in to the currency pressures which have been afflicting the region since early July.
"Theoretically, it's a free float," bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the adaptment period.
"You can also call it a managed float without a band."

The rupiah dove on the news, plunging about four percent or more than 100 points after opening at 2,648/58 against the dollar. In the mid-afternoon, it was trading at 2,750/60 and appeared to have temporarily stabilised, dealers said.

The bank had last fixed the intervention band at 2,378/2,682 on Wednesday. Under the previous system of exchange rate management, the rupiah was allowed to fluctuate within an intervention band whose mid-point was set on a daily basis by the central bank.
The rupiah has fallen about 17 percent in the year so far, compared with an unofficial government target of four-to-five percent annual depreciation.
On July 1, the rupiah was trading at around 2,430 against the dollar although subsequent pressures took it down to a record low of 2,665 on July 21 and then 2,682 on Wednesday.
Dealers said the market was still looking for a new equilibrium level and much could depend on how traders in London and New York reacted to the news.

Indonesian stocks, already suffering from the lingering problems in regional currency markets, were hammered by the news of the float, with the composite index diving 2.37 percent to a 13-week low of 643.01 points.
The index has dropped almost 80 points since the beginning of the month.

Djiwandono noted that the Thai baht and the Philippine peso had been floated since speculative attacks on regional currencies began, while the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore dollar were being traded without any pre-announced limits.
"We are a regional market now. We are moving together," Djiwandono said.
"In the last few weeks Indonesia is the only one which had a band, it's the only one defending the rupiah," he said adding that maintaining that position would be more and more difficult.
"We are adjusting to the new realities," he said. "The new reality in the ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) region is floating (currencies)."
Economists were confident that healthy economic fundamentals would help the currency recover.
"It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, regional currencies specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore.
"Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth."
He said it was not surprising the rupiah had plunged on the announcement but said there was scope for recovery later.

"We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But it (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value."
Some market-watchers said it was possible that after abandoning the intervention band, Indonesia could introduce some form of mild capital controls to limit the scope for speculation.
Both Malaysia and Singapore have adopted systems which prevent sizeable non-trade forward transactions.
But Djiwandono said there would be no move to introduce exchange controls on the rupiah.
"Why should we control?" he said when asked if there was a possibility of any such move."
